sections.text: WS-POL-C – Scope, Triaging, and Policy Crosswalk Analysis

The strongest overall conclusion is that WS-POL-C is where the committee moved from values to architecture: not just what FCCPS believes, but what the AI policy is actually about, which risks it must explicitly cover, and how much of the work belongs in new AI policy versus existing FCCPS policy, regulation, guidance, procurement, and legal compliance structures. The public record shows stronger convergence on a broad, challenge-based framing than on a settled answer to every scoping choice. It also shows a real split between a narrower GenAI/detectors-first focus and a broader AI-enabled-systems / governance / wellbeing focus. (GitHub)

heading_path: How the committee got to WS-POL-C
sections.text: Meeting 3 appears to be the key turning point. Thomas Colvin said the committee’s earlier assumptions, misconceptions, and use cases “crossed boundaries,” and that most of them were better understood as challenges rather than settled truths. He then named several of the challenges that later became the backbone of Section C: uncertain benefits, new risks, student and educator access regardless of school policy, and the difficulty of knowing when AI has been used. He also explicitly said the committee had focused “a lot” on academic integrity but less on other risks, including students being less likely to reach out to a person for mental health support and students generating harmful media about peers or teachers. John Black then reinforced that the committee’s task was to reduce uncertainty enough to create policy that is useful and flexible, and suggested the committee might need to “agree on the problems, if not the solutions.” (GitHub)

heading_path: How the committee got to WS-POL-C
sections.text: Elizabeth Chua pushed the same discussion in a slightly different direction: scope should not be driven by AI “in itself,” but by what students should learn, by grade bands, and by IB-aligned learning goals. That move matters for WS-POL-C because it implies that scope should be broad enough to capture the real risks and uses of AI, but still filtered through educational purpose rather than technology fascination. In other words, the question is not merely “How much AI do we cover?” but “Which AI-related issues change educational decision-making enough that the Board needs explicit guidance?” (GitHub)

heading_path: How the committee got to WS-POL-C
sections.text: The Values & Principles guidance packet shows that this was deliberate process design, not incidental drift. The packet says the goal was to produce a small set of board-ready principles and at least one tradeoff statement, and that workstreams exist to protect the process from single-lens dominance across instruction, assessment, equity, privacy/security, governance, communications, and implementation. That framing helps explain why WS-POL-C exists as a distinct section in V3: it is the place where the committee decides which of those domains belong inside the AI policy shell, which belong in cross-references, and which belong in supporting guidance rather than in the Board-facing policy core. (GitHub)

heading_path: How the committee got to WS-POL-C
sections.text: The Shared Baseline strengthens that reading. It says the policy’s purpose is to guide how students learn to use AI, how schools integrate AI into teaching, how AI may support personalized learning, and how FCCPS captures benefits and mitigates risks and community concerns. It also says policy should be evidence-informed, IB-aligned, and age-appropriate. That is already a broader mandate than “cheating and detectors.” It suggests the committee started from a whole-system frame, even though later drafting tensions pulled some members toward a narrower GenAI-centered view. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 3: How broad should the policy scope be?
sections.text: The clearest documentary evidence of the unresolved scope question is the outline itself. In V3, Decision 3 asks whether policy should focus primarily on GenAI and related detectors or should speak more broadly to AI-enabled systems used in FCCPS contexts. That wording captures the committee’s actual divide well. One possible scope is tight: GenAI, detectors, disclosure, integrity, and selected classroom uses. The other is broad: classroom tools, operational systems, vendor tools, identity-linked platforms, workflow tools, and school-facing AI uses that may not look like ChatGPT but still materially affect students or staff.

heading_path: Decision 3: How broad should the policy scope be?
sections.text: The strongest evidence for the broader scope comes from the committee’s governance-oriented workstreams. Jillian Burkley’s D-DPS draft says every AI tool used in FCCPS classrooms or operations should be classified into one of three risk tiers based on how it handles student data. It then adds escalation rules for identity-linked tools, consequential uses, and student work artifacts, and crosswalks approval requirements to FERPA, IDEA/Section 504/ADA, COPPA, Virginia student-data privacy law, DPA review, vendor security assessment, and procurement workflows. That is not a GenAI-only frame. It is a system-wide AI governance frame.

heading_path: Decision 3: How broad should the policy scope be?
sections.text: The equity workstream points the same way. D-EQA-1 says its checklist should apply not just to classroom use, but to policy language, guidance, tools, and workflows. Its “Scope of Review” asks reviewers to specify target users (students, staff, families), settings (in-class, homework, assessment, IEP/504, ELL, other), and data touched. Its rapid triage includes access, disability, language, enforcement fairness, safety/wellbeing, privacy/data/records, staff capacity, and vendor bias/testing questions. That is clearly broader than a GenAI-only or integrity-only policy scope. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 3: How broad should the policy scope be?
sections.text: The strongest evidence for the narrower scope is less institutional and more reactive. In the survey export, one respondent argued that it would be “impracticable” to require the school to maintain a public registry of every AI tool in use and said bluntly, “The core issue is GEN AI.” The same response warned that broader notice/consent structures would become an “implementation nightmare” without “a much tighter focus.” That is the clearest documented articulation of the narrow-scope faction: focus on the AI uses that most directly change student learning, integrity, and authorship, and do not let the policy sprawl into every adaptive or AI-assisted system in the district. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 3: How broad should the policy scope be?
sections.text: There is also a subtler narrow-scope tendency visible in the public drafting pattern. D-POL-1’s early policy shell centers its idealized goals, decisions, and constraints on GenAI specifically, not on AI-enabled systems in general. That does not prove that any one named member wanted a narrow scope, but it does show that one influential drafting stream initially organized the Board-facing policy around the most visible and controversial AI category. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 3: How broad should the policy scope be?
sections.text: My reading of member positions is therefore this: Thomas Colvin appears to favor a broad, challenge-first scope, because he explicitly insisted the committee must account for risks beyond academic integrity, including mental health and offensive media. Jillian Burkley clearly favors a broad governance scope, because D-DPS covers all AI tools in classrooms or operations rather than only GenAI. Elizabeth Chua supports broad scope in principle, but filtered through learning goals and grade bands, which may make her practically narrower than the governance camp. The public record shows some committee members or respondents pulling toward a much tighter GenAI-centered focus, but I found less direct named-discussion evidence for that view than for the broader governance lens. (GitHub)

heading_path: Triaging: how should the policy sort uses and risks?
sections.text: On triaging, the committee appears to agree much more strongly on the need for triage than on how elaborate it should be. D-DPS is the clearest example: it proposes a three-tier risk framework with escalators for identity linkage, consequential use, and student artifacts, then ties each tier to approval requirements. D-EQA uses a different but complementary triage model: green/yellow/red ratings across access, disability, language, integrity fairness, safety/wellbeing, privacy, staff capacity, and vendor checks. D-CPX adds a third flavor by offering illustrative, not prescriptive scenarios and saying educators must retain case-by-case discretion even where values and principles are shared. Together, those documents show that triaging was not controversial as an idea; what remained controversial was how centralized, formal, and burdensome it should become. (GitHub)

heading_path: Triaging: how should the policy sort uses and risks?
sections.text: The survey captures that disagreement clearly. One respondent supported clearer demarcation of allowed, conditional, and prohibited uses but repeatedly objected that terms like “AI pilot project,” “new use,” “expansion,” and “risk-based limit” were too vague and would invite bureaucratic wrangling. The same response preferred a single continuous-improvement policy over layered pilot/off-ramp structures. That suggests the real fault line is not “triage or no triage,” but structured triage versus lightweight triage: should FCCPS use formal categories, checklists, and decision pathways, or should it rely more on higher-level principles and local judgment? (GitHub)

heading_path: Triaging: how should the policy sort uses and risks?
sections.text: This also maps onto member styles. The governance workstreams tend toward formal triage with criteria, the classroom-practice workstream tends toward illustrative triage with discretion, and the process-centered voices in Meeting 3 tend toward triage anchored in clearly stated problems. That suggests you can fairly write WS-POL-C as showing agreement on the necessity of triage, while preserving disagreement about whether that triage should take the form of district-wide categories, guidance libraries, procurement checklists, or looser problem-based review. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: This is where the public record is clearest about inclusion and less clear about how far inclusion should go. Meeting 3 explicitly surfaced non-academic risks: Thomas Colvin said the committee had spent a lot of time on academic integrity and much less on risks such as students being less likely to reach out to a person for mental health support and students generating offensive media about peers or teachers. In V3, that concern becomes Decision 4, which asks whether the policy should address non-academic AI risks including mental health, harassment, manipulative interaction, and quasi-social dependence. So the committee did not stumble into these issues later; they were named as a deliberate scoping question. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: The workstreams reinforce that these are not fringe concerns. D-EQA’s rapid triage includes safety / wellbeing, asks whether a use exposes students to harmful content or risky contact, and treats enforcement fairness, privacy, and staff capacity as equity questions too. D-DPS’s special-considerations section treats behavioral and counseling-related data as especially sensitive and warns that monitoring systems can amplify bias and drive high-stakes consequences. That means at least two workstreams were already thinking about student wellbeing, behavior, vulnerable groups, and non-academic harms as part of the policy universe, not as unrelated side issues. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: External sources make this scoping choice easier to defend. Virginia’s official AI education guidelines say AI integration in education should “do no harm,” prioritize integrity, and never replace human judgment; they also explicitly tie responsible integration to existing policy and IT standards and to harms affecting individuals, relationships, and communities. APS’s public guidance similarly gives AI policy a wider remit than academics alone, with explicit sections on personal & social wellbeing, equity, transparency, accountability, and privacy, security & safety, including prevention of harm in bullying and harassment contexts.

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: There are also current youth-specific signals that non-academic risks are not hypothetical. Common Sense Media’s 2025 companion-bot assessment concluded that popular social AI companions should not be used by minors and described emotional attachment, harmful advice, role-play, and unsafe interactions as serious concerns. Stanford’s August 2025 report on AI companions and young people likewise warned that these systems can exploit teenagers’ emotional needs and argued for stronger restriction and safeguards for youth. Those sources do not dictate FCCPS policy, but they support the committee members who wanted mental-health, manipulative-interaction, and quasi-social-dependence risks surfaced explicitly rather than buried under academic integrity language alone. (Common Sense Media)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: What I found less clearly documented is how much of this the committee wanted in Board policy itself versus in guidance, implementation, or risk registers. The evidence is stronger that members wanted these risks recognized than that they had converged on how extensively to codify them. That makes Decision 4 a genuine drafting judgment call rather than a settled committee consensus. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: Policy crosswalk: what belongs in new AI policy versus existing FCCPS policy?

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: The accessible record suggests the policy crosswalk issue is more structural than ideological. V3 says Section C should identify where existing FCCPS policies already govern related conduct, identify where AI changes scale, ambiguity, evidentiary conditions, or operational burden enough to require additional guidance, and recommend an appendix or crosswalk listing policies that should be reviewed, clarified, or updated. That language strongly implies that the committee did not intend the AI policy to replace the district’s whole policy architecture. It intended AI policy to overlay and clarify it.

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: D-DPS is the strongest evidence of that overlay model. The deliverable depends on existing DPA templates and procurement workflows, calls for legal review of Virginia student-data privacy law, and repeatedly maps AI tool decisions to preexisting federal and state regimes such as FERPA, IDEA, Section 504/ADA, and COPPA. D-EQA points the same way from an implementation angle: when a risk is found, reviewers are told to decide whether the mitigation lives in policy, guidance, professional development, tool governance, or something else. That is a crosswalk mindset, not a “one AI policy does everything” mindset. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: The public readiness snapshot suggests this part of the work was still maturing. It shows D-POL-1, D-DPS-1, D-EQA-1, and D-CPX-1 in progress, but D-CCI-1 and D-IPC-1 still not started in the public view. So the committee had begun to build the technical and equity crosswalks, but had not yet fully worked through the communications and implementation implications in the public record. That is one reason I would be careful not to overstate committee-wide agreement on the final form of the appendix/crosswalk, even though the need for one is clearly signaled in the outline. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: Best characterization of the range of opinions

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: The range of opinion on WS-POL-C appears to run along three main axes.

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: First, on scope breadth, one position favors a tighter policy centered on GenAI, detectors, integrity, and the most visibly disruptive classroom uses; another favors a broader policy encompassing AI-enabled systems, operations, vendor tools, wellbeing risks, and governance structures. The public record is stronger on the existence of the broader camp than on named advocates for the narrower one, though the survey contains a clear narrow-scope statement. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: Second, on triaging, one position favors formal, district-wide categories and checklists; another favors illustrative guidance and educator discretion; and a third wants triage language simplified enough to avoid bureaucratic overgrowth. The record supports saying these are differences of operational style more than differences over whether risk differentiation is needed. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: Third, on non-academic risks, the committee clearly recognized these issues, but the public evidence does not show a settled view on how much of them should be codified in policy text versus handled elsewhere. This is likely the most open-ended part of Section C and the place where drafting choices will matter most. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: What this means for your drafting

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: For your draft, the safest committee-grounded common-ground language is: FCCPS needs a policy scope that is broad enough to capture the real educational, operational, privacy, equity, and wellbeing risks AI creates, but disciplined enough to remain governable; AI policy should be interpreted alongside existing FCCPS policy and should extend or clarify existing rules where AI changes scale, ambiguity, evidence, or implementation burden. That is very well supported by the public record. (GitHub)

heading_path: Decision 4: Should the policy explicitly cover non-academic AI risks?
sections.text: Where you will have to choose your own position is on three narrower questions: whether to make the Board-facing policy explicitly about AI-enabled systems broadly or still speak mainly in the language of GenAI and detectors; whether Decision 4 should list non-academic harms prominently or defer most of them to supporting guidance; and how much the crosswalk should push specific changes to existing FCCPS policies versus simply recommending review and clarification. The accessible record gives you ample basis to adopt a broader, governance-aware, challenge-based framing if that is your preference, while also acknowledging the narrower-scope concern that the policy can become too diffuse to implement cleanly.

title: How the committee got to WS-POL-C
